idiom_name: owned assignment (*self = new_value) plus std::mem::swap/replace as the commit
implementation_notes: Rust's assignment already has the copy-and-swap ordering built in: the right-hand side is evaluated to a complete value first, and only then is the old value dropped and the new one moved into the place, so a panic -- or an abort, or a failed Clone -- while building leaves the target untouched. std::mem::swap, replace and take are the non-failing commit primitives when the old value must be handed on or returned, Clone (or a bespoke with_x method) plays the copy constructor's role, and Drop releases the old state with no explicit cleanup step. Hand-rolled copies of the C++ structure are only needed at boundaries the borrow checker cannot express: committing into a place you do not own (&mut through FFI or MaybeUninit), prising one field out of a struct, or implementing both the value and its previous contents. The failure model differs in kind -- panics and aborts, not exceptions -- so unwind safety replaces exception safety.
pitfalls: Panics are the failure mode, not exceptions: with panic = 'abort' there is no unwinding at all, and with unwinding the guarantee holds only for unwind-safe types -- catch_unwind needs UnwindSafe evidence before it can turn a panic back into a rollback.

mem::swap and replace need unique access; interior mutability (RefCell, Mutex) moves the aliasing check to run time, where a conflicting borrow panics and a Mutex poisoned by a panicking writer returns Err.
clone() on a type holding Rc/Arc shares the interior: the copy is shallow where the C++ copy constructor would have deep-copied, so the guarantee survives but value semantics do not.
mem::replace/take demand a real replacement value; faking one with MaybeUninit or unsafe reintroduces the destroy-before-construct window and can leak or double-drop.
